s.c: Since prostitution is an almost universal behavioral trait, it is not difficult to obtain terms for such a person or activity. The difficulty is usually involved in selecting a term which will not be vulgar. Expressions for a prostitute are often idiomatic, for example, ‘one who acts like a she-dog,’ ‘one who sells her vulva,’ ‘one who sells herself,’ or ‘one who receives any man.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sexual Misbehavior

However, in all languages it is possible to be somewhat more precise about color terms by likening the color to that of a local flower or bird.

liquids used for nourishment or to satisfy thirst
s.c: Though in many languages the equivalent of πόσις and πόμα would be a verbal derivative meaning basically ‘that which is drunk,’ in other languages the equivalent may be ‘watery food’ or ‘liquid food.’|In some languages, however, one cannot refer to ‘blood’ (⟦John 6:55|John 6:55⟧) as being ‘drink,’ since blood is classified as food rather than as drink. On the other hand, it may be possible to translate ‘my blood is the real drink’ as ‘my blood is real nourishment.’ The expression ‘food and drink’ (⟦Hebrews 9:10|Hebrews 9:10⟧) may be better rendered in some languages as ‘all kinds of food.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: consumption of liquids, particularly water and wine
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between drinking water and drinking alcoholic beverages. Still other terms may be employed in speaking of drinking soups or broths.

s.d: interrogative of quantity of objects or events, usually implying a considerable amount
interrogative of quantity
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary in ⟦Luke 16:5|Luke 16:5⟧ to employ an expression relating to countable objects, for example, ‘how many pieces of money do you owe my master?’ (see LN 59.5).

s.d: a relatively high point on a scale involving exclamation
s.g: how; very; how great; how much; intense; severe
s.c: In a number of languages an expression of high degree in an exclamation can only be reproduced as an expression of intensive degree in a non-exclamatory form. For example, the statement in ⟦Matthew 6:23|Matthew 6:23⟧ ‘how great must the darkness be!’ must be rendered in a number of languages as ‘the darkness is very, very intense’ or ‘it is very, very dark there.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water

an object from which one may drink
s.c: In place of the expression ‘cup of water’ (in which cup not only identifies the container but indicates the quantity of water), some languages would use the expression ‘water in a cup,’ but it is even more likely that the typical equivalent of ‘cup of water’ would be ‘a drink of water.’ In some parts of the world a term such as ‘cup’ would suggest something rather strange and foreign; therefore, one might find that an expression ‘a gourd of water’ would not only be more natural, but would be the semantic equivalent of ‘drink of water.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to take the cup … from) to cause someone to not undergo some trying experience

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering

s.g: to undergo a difficult experience; to drink the cup; to suffer
s.c: In a number of languages it is not possible to use the phrase ‘to drink the cup,’ since this will almost inevitably refer to the drinking of a poison cup as a means of proving innocence in an ordeal. Even if one uses a literal rendering of the idiom ‘to drink the cup,’ it is usually necessary to have some explanation as to the significance of the idiom.

s.c: In ⟦Revelation 10:1|Revelation 10:1⟧ (οἱ πόδες αὐτοῦ ὡς στῦλοι πυρός ‘his feet were like pillars of fire’) it is possible that πούς refers to the leg since the context of ⟦Revelation 10:1|Revelation 10:1⟧ would seem to favor this interpretation, but the meaning of ‘foot’ should not be excluded, especially since this passage refers to an image as part of a supernatural vision, and one cannot be certain of the specific intent.

s.d: (idioms, literally under the feet of, and:  footstool of the feet) to be under the complete control of someone
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that ⟦1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25⟧ might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

The πραιτώριον in Caesarea was the palace built by Herod the Great (see ⟦Acts 23:35|Acts 23:35⟧).|In the Gospels it is satisfactory to translate πραιτώριον as ‘the palace where the governor lived’ or ‘the large dwelling where the ruler lived.’ In a number of languages a term for ‘palace’ often suggests a military fortification, and this would accordingly be quite appropriate for NT usage.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Grow, Growth
s.d: to begin vegetative growth, with special emphasis upon the sprouting of leaves
s.c: The initial stages of growth, either of a plant as a whole or in the renewal of foliage after a winter or dry season, may be expressed in a number of ways, for example, ‘to become green again,’ ‘to show leaves,’ ‘to see leaves begin,’ or ‘when leaves unfold.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:πρόβατον<SDBG:πρόβατον:000000>} ‘sheep,’ {D:4.22}) pertaining to sheep
s.c: The phrase ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ is an elliptical expression in which the noun for ‘gate’ (which is feminine in gender) is omitted. The phrase ‘at the Sheep Gate’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘close to the gate of the city through which sheep entered’ or ‘… were driven’ or ‘… were led.’

s.d: herbivorous domestic mammal with four legs; Ovis ladicaudata - fat-tailed sheep; used for sacrifice, source of meat, milk, hides, wool, and horns
s.c: Since the distribution of sheep throughout the world is somewhat less than that of goats, there may be more difficulties involved in finding an adequate term. In some instances terms for sheep are actually based upon a term for goat. For example, among Eskimos goats are well known because there are wild goats in the mountains, and sheep are accordingly called in some dialects ‘woolly goats’ or ‘goats that have wool.’ Among the Maya in Yucatan sheep were introduced by the Spanish and were first described as being ‘cotton deer,’ and the name still persists. In some areas where sheep are not known at all, the meat of sheep is known, and accordingly sheep may be called by the name of the meat, for example, ‘mutton animals.’ But in most places where sheep are not indigenous, there is nevertheless some term for them, usually based upon a borrowing from a dominant language.|For the translator, however, there are often problems involving the connotations of the term for sheep and for related expressions concerning their behavior and the ways in which they are ‘led.’ As already noted under the discussion of goats (LN 4.19), sheep are frequently less prized than goats, and therefore it may seem strange in biblical texts to find sheep being given a preferential rating. What may appear even more difficult to understand is the suggestion that sheep are led by a shepherd rather than being driven. This fact may require some type of marginal note to accompany the text if people are to understand the basis for a number of similes and metaphors of the Scriptures. Furthermore, if the experience which people have of sheep is only their knowledge about wild sheep, then obviously references to the helplessness of sheep will be either meaningless or even contradictory. Again, a marginal note is in order.

s.d: to happen or occur previous to some point of time

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer

s.d: to know about something prior to some temporal reference point, for example, to know about an event before it happens
s.g: to know beforehand; to know already; to have foreknowledge

s.d: (derivative of {L:προγινώσκω<SDBG:προγινώσκω:000000>}[a] ‘to know beforehand,’ {D:28.6}) that which is known ahead of time or before a particular temporal reference

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations

s.d: to write in advance or in anticipation of
to provide information in a vivid manner
s.c: It would be wrong to assume that προγράφω in ⟦Galatians 3:1|Galatians 3:1⟧ refers to some kind of theatrical demonstration. The portrayal mentioned here was evidently a vivid verbal description.

s.d: pertaining to being easily seen and known by the public

s.g: to give beforehand; to give in advance; to give first
s.c: It is possible to render ⟦Romans 11:35|Romans 11:35⟧ as ‘who has ever given God something before God gave something?’

s.d: (derivative of προδίδωμι ‘to betray,’ not occurring in the NT) one who delivers without justification a person into the control of someone else
(a figurative extension of meaning of πρόδρομος ‘one who runs on ahead,’ not occurring in the NT) one who undergoes an experience in advance of others
s.c: In rendering πρόδρομος in ⟦Hebrews 6:20|Hebrews 6:20⟧ it is important to avoid an expression which would suggest that Jesus simply ‘ran on ahead.’ The implication of πρόδρομος in this type of context is that of a precursor, that is to say, one who goes on ahead in order to show the way or to pioneer on behalf of someone else. ⟦Hebrews 6:20|Hebrews 6:20⟧ may therefore be rendered as ‘Jesus went on ahead of us in there for our benefit.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Hope, Look Forward To
s.d: to hope in a prior manner, either beforehand or prior to someone else
s.g: to hope beforehand; to be the first to hope

s.d: to begin an activity previously
to announce with certainty in advance as to what one will do
to continue to move forward{N:001}
s.g: to move on; to go on; to go ahead

s.dp: Linear Movement › Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
s.d: to move continuously along a particular path or route
s.g: to pass along; to go along
s.c: It is also possible to interpret ῥύμην μίαν in ⟦Acts 12:10|Acts 12:10⟧ as referring to a particular section or block in a street; therefore, one may translate ‘they went one street further.’

s.d: to come/go prior to some other event, normally one involving a similar type of movement
s.g: to come/go prior to; to come/go beforehand; to precede
s.c: Though the movement referred to by φθάνω and προέρχομαι may involve movement which is spacially ahead of someone else, nevertheless the focus of meaning is not a spacial relationship but a temporal one.

s.d: to go in front of, in order to show the way
s.g: to lead; to show the way to

s.d: to make ready or prepare in advance
s.g: to make ready in advance; to prepare in advance

s.d: to spread good news in advance of its happening (in the NT, restricted in reference to the good news about Jesus Christ)
s.g: to bring the good news ahead of time

s.d: to experience superior benefit or advantage, implying some type of comparison
s.g: to have a greater benefit; to experience a superior advantage
s.c: In indicating ‘a superior advantage’ it may be necessary to be quite specific about the basis for the comparison. For example, in ⟦1 Corinthians 8:8|1 Corinthians 8:8⟧ it may be necessary to translate as ‘if we do eat, we will be no better off than if we did not eat,’ and in ⟦Romans 3:9|Romans 3:9⟧ one may translate ‘what then; are we decidedly better off than the others are?’

s.d: to do something with eagerness
s.c: For another interpretation of προηγέομαι in ⟦Romans 12:10|Romans 12:10⟧, see LN 78.35.

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: to exhibit a type of behavior far above the norm
s.c: In ⟦Romans 12:10|Romans 12:10⟧ προηγέομαι serves primarily to indicate the degree of showing honor. One could therefore translate this expression as ‘honor one another to an exceptional degree.’ For another interpretation of προηγέομαι in ⟦Romans 12:10|Romans 12:10⟧, see LN 68.70.

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: (derivative of προτίθεμαι[a] ‘to plan in advance,’ {D:30.62}) that which is planned or purposed in advance
(an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
s.g: bread offered to God; consecrated bread
s.c: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
s.d: some point of time selected in advance

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: eagerness to engage in some activity or event
s.c: A phrase such as ‘with all eagerness’ (⟦Acts 17:11|Acts 17:11⟧) must often be expressed as a clause, for example, ‘and were very eager.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: pertaining to being eager to do something
s.c: It would be wrong to equate the meaning of πρόθυμος and προθύμως with ἑκούσιος, ἑκών, and ἑκουσίως (LN 25.65), for πρόθυμος and προθύμως imply far more desire and eagerness, though both sets of terms are often translated in English as ‘willing’ or ‘willingly.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: pertaining to being eager to do something
s.c: It would be wrong to equate the meaning of πρόθυμος and προθύμως with ἑκούσιος, ἑκών, and ἑκουσίως (LN 25.65), for πρόθυμος and προθύμως imply far more desire and eagerness, though both sets of terms are often translated in English as ‘willing’ or ‘willingly.’

s.d: to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
s.g: to guide; to direct; to lead
s.c: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.|The phrase ‘in the Lord’ in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:12|1 Thessalonians 5:12⟧ probably refers to matters concerning the Christian life.

s.d: to be engaged in helping or aiding
s.g: to be active in helping; to be involved in giving aid

s.d: to engage in something with intense devotion
s.g: to strive for; to devote oneself to

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to cause provocation or irritation in someone
to announce openly what is to happen in the future
to make ready or prepare in advance
s.g: to make ready in advance; to prepare in advance

s.d: to exist in an evident manner
s.g: to exist openly; to exist clearly

s.d: to exist subsequent to some temporal reference point
s.g: to exist later; to lie before (someone); to lie ahead

s.d: to preach in anticipation or in advance

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to change one’s state for the better by advancing and making progress
s.g: to advance; to progress; to change for the better; advancement

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to change one’s state for the better by advancing and making progress
s.g: to advance; to progress; to change for the better; advancement

s.d: to progress or advance in some activity
s.g: to progress; to advance; to accomplish

s.d: to cause a significant increase in some quantity
s.c: This expression in ⟦2 Timothy 2:16|2 Timothy 2:16⟧ may be rendered in some languages as ‘they cause people to be more and more godless’ or ‘… to do what God does not want them to do.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
s.g: to draw near; to draw to a close

s.d: to make a decision based upon unjustified preference, with the implication of prejudging
s.g: to show partiality; to decide unfairly; to judge prejudicially; partiality; prejudice
s.c: It may be necessary in some languages to define the implications of ‘prejudice’ by saying ‘to decide against someone without any reason’ or ‘to decide against someone without knowing what is true.’
